5.0.s.en: (1) Introduction to the Sermon on the Mount

5.0.0.en: The crowds multiplied behind Christ, so He went out with them to the mountain to speak to them with His life-giving words.

5.0.1.en: The mountain points spiritually to rising above material things, and to spiritual strength and steadfastness. He spoke to them in a long discourse that took up three chapters, and it is regarded as a constitution of Christianity containing its most important teachings. His disciples drew near to Him because of their love for Him.

5.0.2.en: "Went up": there were many crowds following Christ, those mentioned at the end of the previous chapter. So that they might hear Him and see Him clearly, He went up a short distance on the mountain and sat down, and His disciples came to Him. As for the rest of the crowds, they sat before Him on the ground in the wide valley; and this mountain is one of the mountains near Capernaum in Galilee.

5.1.0.en: Christ began to speak and teach the crowds in direct words, and this sermon is one of His most famous. He may have repeated some of its meanings on other occasions, but because of its importance it is regarded as a constitution of Christianity. His sermon served as an interpretation of the Law, adding to it the perfection of the Christian life, for He did not come to destroy the Law but to fulfil it (v. 17).

5.2.s.en: (2) The Beatitudes, which are the blessings

5.2.0.en: Christ began His discourse by encouraging His children and praising them, so that they would strive in their spiritual life, so He showed them the reward, that they might be zealous for spiritual work.

5.2.1.en: The first praise was for "the poor in spirit", that is, the humble, because humility is the foundation of every virtue, just as pride is the first sin that made Adam fall, and Satan also. Consequently, the humble person is assured of the eternal Kingdom of Heaven by God's dwelling in his heart with His spiritual Kingdom, so he rejoices and enjoys it at all times.

5.3.0.en: Then He praises those who mourn for their sins, that is, the penitent, and those who grieve over the sins of others and so pray for them, because God gives them peace in their hearts in this life, and then heavenly comforts and glories in eternity.

5.3.1.en: For this reason the children of God loved tears and remorse over sin, so that they might live in righteousness with tender hearts that feel God's compassion and forgiveness and thank Him at all times. This mourning is of course different from grief over the loss of material things, or not obtaining them; that is vain grief from which one must be freed.

5.4.0.en: When a person is adorned with repentance, his soul grows calm, so he becomes meek within, not stirred by any gain or loss. In proportion to the strength of the spirit's relationship with God, the body grows calm and its energies are disciplined; and Christ presented Himself as the highest example of meekness for us to learn from Him.

5.4.1.en: Some think that the meek person loses his rights in this life, but God promises the meek that they shall inherit the earth. What is meant by "the earth" is not only the new earth in the Kingdom of Heaven, but also the earth on which we live, for the meek person is loved by everyone and God's blessings to him increase, material as well as spiritual, so he lacks nothing material.

5.4.2.en: The earth also signifies the body, which submits to the spirit and becomes a temple of the Holy Spirit.

5.4.3.en: The earth also signifies the wicked, who turn from their evil nature through contact with the meek, and in this way they are won for Christ.

5.5.0.en: "Righteousness": it is goodness and good works, and all life in God. The perfection of righteousness is Christ, so hungering and thirsting after Him is the feeling of constant need to be filled with Him. Just as the children of Israel in the wilderness had their hunger satisfied by God with manna from heaven and their thirst quenched with water from the rock, giving them life in the barren wilderness, so Christ is our life, which we cannot live without Him. And whoever seeks Christ will surely be filled and full of joy.

5.5.1.en: This hunger and thirst drives a person to grow in the spiritual life through aspiration and increasing nearness to God, and seizing every opportunity to know Him through prayer, reading and meditation, and above all enjoying the Holy Sacraments.

5.6.0.en: Mercy is feeling for the other and putting yourself in his place, so you give him, not only material or emotional needs, but participation, so you eat and move and think with him, as Christ did when He became incarnate and shared with us all of our nature except sin alone. And remember that Christ is the one with whom you are doing mercy, because He called the needy "His brethren", and what we do for them is as though we had done it for Him. The reward of mercy is that we obtain God's mercies in our life, especially in tribulation, and then in eternal bliss (see ch. 10:42, ch. 25:34-46).

5.7.0.en: "Heart": it represents the inside of a person, his depths, feelings and intentions, and its purity means its being stripped of every evil desire and every worldly preoccupation that distracts from the love of God, for the heart becomes prepared for God's dwelling through purity, and is able to see God and feel that He is within it and with it in everything, not by sensory sight or hearing, but by spiritual perception, because it is deeper than sensory things, and very satisfying to the soul; and all the preceding qualities come together to qualify the soul for the purity by which we see God.

5.8.0.en: "Peace": it is the steadiness of the heart, its rest and joy. Making peace begins with oneself, so I live in peace, and this requires giving up everything that disturbs, of bad desires and earthly greed, indeed being ready to give up all rights and keep the most important right, which is inner peace.

5.8.1.en: And if we have gained our peace, we can make peace with others through love and prayers for them, and helping them out of their troubles, even if we bear with them much because they are poor souls who have lost their peace. Peace is submission to God, the God of heaven, who grants it as a gift to those who love Him. And He made peace between earth and heaven, and a reconciliation between them, by His blood on the Cross. If we strive to seek peace, we are truly His children.

5.9.0.en: The eighth and last beatitude results from all the seven preceding qualities, and it is enduring persecutions for the sake of the pure life and faithfulness, and for the sake of obeying Christ and His commandments. And the Lord promises us, in return for the limited sufferings of this life, the glories of the Kingdom of Heaven which never end. "Righteousness": that is, goodness and works of good and life with God, and this is a condition for the heavenly reward, because if people wrong us not for our righteousness but for mistakes that we made, this is our natural recompense.

5.9.1.en: "Revile": that is, mock you and your Christ and all your beliefs and upright conduct.

5.9.2.en: "All manner of evil": these are false accusations that the wicked claim against you, as they did in the days of the Roman persecution, and in every generation.

5.9.3.en: "Rejoice, and be exceeding glad": because you have shared with Christ in His sufferings, and because of the heavenly glories that await you in return for all that you endured.

5.9.4.en: "Great": to show the measure of the heavenly blessings that cannot be expressed.

5.9.5.en: And He calls us to confidence in our righteous conduct, whatever doubts and claims of the wicked we endure, knowing that they are our way to receive our heavenly reward, especially as all the prophets and saints endured for God's sake, for endurance is an essential condition for obtaining the Kingdom.

5.9.6.en: And the texts of these beatitudes are the qualities of the Christian person, none of which can be dispensed with in order to obtain the eight rewards.

5.9.7.en: And before us is our highest example, Christ, so that we may find the practical application of all these qualities in Him.

5.9.8.en: If you seek happiness and long to reach the Kingdom, you must acquire virtue, and labor to acquire it, and so rejoice in Christ's dwelling in you.

5.9.9.en: Examine your life, to know the recurring sin that you suffer from, and strive to acquire the virtue that is the opposite of your sin. If you suffer from pride, learn humility. If you are fought by impurity, you need purity ... and the guidance of your father of confession will benefit you greatly in this matter.

5.10.0.en: Christ likened His children to the salt that salts the earth, that is, earthly people bound to the world. Salt is distinguished by dissolving in food, giving it a better taste without canceling its original flavor, like the Christian who influences others so that they come to a better life without losing their own personalities.

5.10.1.en: Salt is cheap and spread easily throughout the whole world, like the humble Christian whose service spreads to every person. Salt is white in color, so it signifies purity and chastity. It is also used to preserve foods from corruption, just as the Christian preserves himself and those around him and establishes them in life with God.

5.10.2.en: The real problem is that the salt on which we rely to set everyone right should spoil. And when does salt spoil? (1) If it is mixed with foreign substances, so that its effect weakens, like the Christian's mixing with the wicked and being influenced by them. (2) If moisture enters it and weakens its saltiness, and this signifies luxury and indulgence in bodily ease and the desires of a corrupt life.

5.10.3.en: (3) If it is mixed with water and an electric current passes through it, it turns into harmful substances such as caustic soda, and this signifies the Christian's submission to the evil powers of the world, such as attachment to the love of money and various desires, which fill his heart and change him from his nature, and he becomes harmful and corrupting to those around him who see him as an example, and so he becomes a stumbling block to them.

5.10.4.en: Then a problem appears, namely: with what shall we salt or set others right? And from another side: what shall we do with this spoiled salt? It has lost its work and the purpose of its existence in life, and nothing awaits it but to be cast out of the Kingdom, and to suffer the pains of being trodden underfoot, that is, eternal torment, and a crushing that never ends.

5.11.0.en: He likens the Christian to the light whose function is to give light to others, and it is distinguished by the following:

5.11.1.en: (1) It guides others on the path of their life.

5.11.2.en: (2) It reveals to them evil and everything that harms them so that they may keep away from it.

5.11.3.en: (3) It helps them to do good, for work is done in the light and not in the darkness.

5.11.4.en: (4) Light is strong, it does not fear the darkness, that is, evil, but rather the darkness flees from it.

5.11.5.en: So the Christian must be in the loftiness of a spiritual life like a city built on a hill, whose light cannot be hidden, like the moon which lights the world with its light that reflects the light of the sun, which is God; He asks us to give light to the whole world by our good life.

5.12.0.en: He also likens the life of the Christian to a lamp (a light or oil lamp) in a house, whose purpose is to light this house, and it is placed on a lampstand or a high place so that its light reaches all parts of the house; and it is illogical to put a measure over the lamp to hide its light.

5.12.1.en: "Bushel": it is a vessel with a narrow mouth and a larger base, used to determine the volume of grain when it is sold, and if it is placed over the lamp it hides its light completely. It signifies material things, mental measurements, and the cares of the world that prevent the light, "the light of the work of the Holy Spirit in us", from going forth to shine for others.

5.13.0.en: He asks us to be an example to others in good works, so that they may see Christ in us, and the work of His Holy Spirit, and so glorify God and be drawn to life with Him; and our purpose in good works should not be pride and the praise of people and our own glory, but we walk in righteousness for God's sake as an example to others, and so draw hearts to the love of God.

5.13.1.en: You have an essential role in the world, which is showing Christ in your words and your conduct in every place you go to or are in. So ask yourself at the end of every day: have I shown Christ in my home and my work and every place I went? so that you repent of your sins and are careful in your conduct, and so gain yourself and those around you.

5.14.0.en: Christ is God, the giver of the Law. Consequently, it is unreasonable that He should destroy what He established, but He became incarnate to fulfil it; how?

5.14.1.en: A) In Him all the types and prophecies in the Old Testament are fulfilled, as Matthew the Evangelist mentions this phrase: "That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets"...

5.14.2.en: B) He Himself fulfills every law on our behalf, since we were unable to fulfill it, as He says to John the Baptist: "it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness" (ch. 3:15).

5.14.3.en: C) He fulfills the Law in our lives by the power of His Holy Spirit, for if we were unable by our own strength to fulfill it, the Holy Spirit supports us and strengthens us.

5.14.4.en: D) He completes the details of the commandments, giving their causes and roots so that we may avoid them; murder, for example, begins with anger, and adultery begins with an evil look.

5.14.5.en: "The law or the prophets": by these he means all the books of the Old Testament.

5.14.6.en: "Verily": it means "Amen", and what is meant is the establishing and confirming of what He will declare in the verse.

5.14.7.en: "Heaven and earth": an expression for the most stable things in the world, to make clear the steadfastness of God's word in the Holy Bible until the end of the ages.

5.14.8.en: "One jot or one tittle": that is, the smallest teaching cannot change.

5.14.9.en: "Till all be fulfilled": until God's plan for the salvation of His children is completed on the day of judgment, and the application of the whole Law is completed, by the glorification of God's children and the torment of the wicked.

5.15.0.en: The scribes and Pharisees kept the Law literally, but they broke it by their deeds.

5.15.1.en: For despite the importance of the letter, what is more important is carrying it out in practice. Whoever neglects the smallest commandment, and knows it, will be the lowest and least person in the Kingdom of the New Testament, that is, the Church, and he must repent quickly so as not to lose his eternity. For whoever breaks one of the commandments and rejects it deliberately has rejected them all. But as for the one who sins through his weakness, repentance wipes away the sins in the sacrament of confession.

5.15.2.en: But whoever joins his teaching of the commandments with doing them in his life, he is called great in the Church and the eternal Kingdom.

5.15.3.en: Then Christ calls His followers to let their righteousness exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, so that they not be content with keeping the letters of the Law, but must apply its commandments practically in their lives, because if they do not apply the Law they will not enter the Kingdom of Heaven.

5.15.4.en: "The least commandments": they are those that concern keeping away from something, or paying careful attention to something small. They are as important as the great commandments such as the Ten Commandments.

5.15.5.en: The scribes and Pharisees: the Jews thought that because of the abundant knowledge of these two groups, they were the greatest example of life with God, so Christ made clear the necessity that the righteousness of anyone who wants to be saved must exceed this theoretical righteousness.

5.15.6.en: May you apply in your life what you say to others before you teach it to someone else, so you experience it and receive its blessing, and your words are more effective on your hearers. All your spiritual knowledge, God gave to you first before you teach it to others. So accept everything you read or hear for practical application, and so you save yourself and those who hear you, for an upright conduct appears in your life that becomes an example to others without your being aware of it.

5.16.0.en: If the Beatitudes spoke of the positive qualities in the Christian person and their rewards, Christ now mentions the negative sins and how to treat them, and takes for example a difficult commandment, which is "Thou shalt not kill", and so He brings its root, which is the sin of anger, because if we keep away from anger, we will of course not kill anyone. The scribes, Pharisees and elders of the Jews used to punish whoever killed deliberately, while the one who killed unintentionally fled to the cities of refuge. They gave no attention to inward anger, but were content with carrying out anger outwardly in murder. And in order that Christ might make clear the seriousness of anger, He said: "Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause", that is, because of vain, passing material things, "shall be in danger of the judgment", the judgment of the small courts that were set up throughout the Jewish land, in which 23 judges from among the elders ordinarily sat, and this judgment could be appealed or reviewed in the higher courts, the greatest of which was the "Sanhedrin" council in Jerusalem, which consisted of seventy of the great elders of Jerusalem, the heads of the Jews, and for this reason it is also called the council of the seventy, and it is the highest council to which all the subordinate councils belong. It was also the greatest Jewish authority making decisions in the religious matters of the Jews, and many of the scribes were also members of this council.

5.16.1.en: What is meant by anger here is inward anger of the heart, without showing any expression of it.

5.16.2.en: As for "whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca", which is a Syriac word expressing contempt joined with anger, this deserves trial by "the council", that is, the Sanhedrin council, which consists of the great elders of Jerusalem.

5.16.3.en: But if a person goes further in his anger and describes his brother as foolish and stupid, he deserves "hell fire".

5.16.4.en: "Gehenna": taken from the valley of Hinnom, into which the remains of sacrifices were thrown, and worms spread in them, and they burned them with fire, so the fire was never put out in this valley. For this reason God likened eternal torment to the fire that is not quenched and the worm that dies not, in the valley of Hinnom, but in a spiritual way that is more tormenting and severe. And here Christ shows His rejection of anger and its seriousness, for even inward anger deserves judgment before God, and consequently any expression of it will lead a person to eternal perdition.

5.17.0.en: Christ declares clearly that prayers and gifts offered to God are not accepted from the angry person, or the one who wrongs others, or the quarrelsome, because God wants the prayers offered from a pure heart full of love.

5.17.1.en: If one of the Jews offered his sacrifice as a gift to God, and then remembered and noticed that there was a quarrel between him and someone, he should not complete the offering of his sacrifice, but first be reconciled with his brother, then return and complete the offering of his sacrifice, so that it may be accepted by God. "Thy brother hath ought against thee": He did not say that you have something against him, so call yourself to account for your duties before your rights.

5.17.2.en: "Leave": it makes clear the importance of reconciliation and offering love before worship, because if the heart is purified by love it is acceptable to God, and so is the worship it offers.

5.17.3.en: "Go thy way": that is, take care to reconcile with your brother even if he has wronged you, as Christ Himself commands, saying: "If thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault" (ch. 18:15).

5.17.4.en: It is necessary to purify the heart of all anger before prayer, whether in the closet of your house or in the church, and especially when partaking of the Holy Sacraments, because your prayers are not accepted if you have not purified your heart.

5.17.5.en: So hasten to reconcile with others, even if they have wronged you, and so win them by love, and do not be troubled by their pride or harshness, but pray for them that anger may be removed from their hearts, and care for your peace before everything.

5.18.0.en: Your "adversary" is the commandments of God, or your conscience which reminds you of God's word, or the Holy Spirit dwelling in you, since you have come into a quarrel with Him because of your falling into evil.

5.18.1.en: "The way": it is this life. If you submit to the voice of the Holy Spirit and the conscience, and obey the commandment, keeping away from anger, malice and all evil, you save yourself and are reconciled with this adversary; but if you are not reconciled with him by submitting to him and repenting, he delivers you to "the judge", who is God the just Judge on the day of judgment, and he sentences you to eternal perdition, and delivers you to "the officer", who are the angels who cast you into prison, that is, eternal torment, and "Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing" (all your debts down to the smallest coin). And because your sin is unlimited, since it is against the unlimited God, its punishment is unlimited, and consequently you remain in eternal torment.

5.18.2.en: May you guard against the sin of anger, and not give yourself excuses to persist in it, but have compassion on others however great their faults, so you protect yourself from the evil results of anger, and regain your peace, and return to your spiritual way that leads to the Kingdom, and win the souls of those around you.

5.19.0.en: Adultery is looking with the intent of lust, and this gives rise to delight in lust in the thought, which leads to falling in deed in its various degrees. Therefore Christ wanted to cut off the sin from its root, which is looking, making clear that it is counted as adultery, so that no one may be lax about his look or thoughts or feelings and think this ordinary, otherwise he will go further and regard even evil touches as ordinary. And if he falls into complete adultery, he may excuse himself, and so the door of repentance is closed before him, because of his laxity and justification of the sin.

5.19.1.en: As for you, O man of God, flee from looking needlessly so that you do not fall into evil sights, as a person flees from a snake or a scorpion.

5.20.0.en: Since a person, because of his weakness, is exposed to falling by looking or by deed, Christ says:

5.20.1.en: If you have fallen into an evil look, pluck out your right eye which has offended you and made you fall into the sin of adultery. And if you have stolen, cut off your right hand which has offended you.

5.20.2.en: What is meant here is not the literal meaning, for what is the difference between the right eye and the left? Rather the right signifies strength and importance, and so it points to the very close friend, or the beloved desire, or anything dear to you like the eye or the hand, which you must keep away from and give up attachment to, so that you do not fall into sin, and your end be eternal torment.

5.20.3.en: Examine, my brother, the sources of your falling into sin, whether adultery or any other sin, and give them up and keep away from them however dear they are to you, so that you gain the salvation of your soul and your eternity.

5.21.0.en: "A writing of divorcement": the husband sits with one of the scribes and has a record of divorce written, which gives the wife freedom to be joined to another.

5.21.1.en: The pagan world allowed divorce for any reason, especially the Greeks among whom debauchery and adultery in their temples had spread. As for the Jews, he had to reconsider and write a bill of divorce, perhaps so that he might go back on his decision, if he felt that his wife would belong to another, and his anger and distress would calm down.

5.21.2.en: As for Christ, He shows the greatness of the sacrament of marriage, that it is a union that cannot be separated, unless one of the parties is joined in adultery, for then he has separated himself from the other and divided this union. But whoever divorces his wife for any other reason makes her commit adultery if she is joined to another, because she is still his wife before God, and the new husband is counted an adulterer because he married another man's wife.

5.21.3.en: And Christ here does not oppose the Law of Moses written in (Deut 24:1) permitting divorce and writing a bill for it, but returns matters to their origin. Moses was compelled, as a result of his people's mixing with the Egyptians and their becoming accustomed to divorce, to set limits for them, that a person should reconsider and write a certificate of it. But this was not God's intention when He created man to be united with the other in the sacrament of marriage, when He said: "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh" (Gen 2:24), and He gave no permission for divorce except in the case of adultery, because it separates the two bodies of the spouses when one of them is joined to another body. Let us sanctify the sacrament of marriage, to rise above the causes of disputes, and try to resolve them by spiritual guidance, repentance, and clinging to the Church.

5.21.6.en: 33- "Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths: 34- But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: 35- Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. 36- Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. 37- But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

5.22.0.en: God permitted His people of old to swear (take oaths) by His name, in order to direct their hearts to His worship, and not to swear by the pagan gods. What He forbade them was forswearing, that is, swearing falsely. The meaning of that is carrying out what they swore, like vows which must be fulfilled when a person utters them, and he promised God to fulfill them.

5.22.1.en: And the scribes and Pharisees used to teach that the oath by the name of the Lord is the one that must be fulfilled, while an oath by anything else can be retracted. This is of course a wrong teaching which Christ opposes here, and corrects in the following verses, teaching not to swear or take oaths at all.

5.23.0.en: In the New Testament the Law is fulfilled by forbidding oaths, because God's name is too exalted to be said for material dealings, but is to be mentioned for worship and for blessing our life.

5.23.1.en: "God's throne": heaven signifies the presence of God because of its loftiness and height, so it suits His exaltedness.

5.23.2.en: "His footstool": the earth and earthly things are lower than heaven, therefore it was called a footstool for God's feet.

5.23.3.en: From another side, we do not own anything in the world, but we are stewards over it, so how do we swear by something we do not own? God alone is able to swear, because He owns everything.

5.23.4.en: And Christ makes clear that we do not own even one hair of our heads, and are unable to change its color.

5.23.5.en: Consequently, it is not right to swear by the life of a person or anything of the creatures in the world; therefore He asks that our speech be simple, free of oaths, that is, we do not need to prove it by an oath, and our answer to others is only yes or no.

5.23.6.en: "Yea, yea; Nay, nay": that is, we do not use the oath, and we declare facts or our agreement with what others say with the word yes, or forbid and refuse what does not suit us with the word "no", without needing to prove that with the words of an oath. "Of evil": that is, the use of the oath is the work of Satan the evil one, for he is the one who brought about lying and deceit, and calls people to swear to prove their lies.

5.23.7.en: Forbidding the oath restrains anger, so that it does not go on to binding decisions, and it is a mark of Christians in their innocence. An oath is not a proof of truthfulness, but the wicked use it in lying to reach their aims. Be careful with your words, so that God's name is in them for blessing, and keep away from lying, and consequently you do not need to prove your statements with false oaths. And do not make light of God's name, or the lives of people, by swearing by them carelessly merely out of the habit of repeating them.

5.24.0.en: In the Old Testament God wanted to establish the idea of divine justice, and the need for redemption, that if a person sinned he needs a man like himself to redeem him. The eye is redeemed by an eye, and the tooth (singular of teeth) is redeemed by a tooth like it. And because sin is unlimited, since it is against God, it needed an unlimited redemption, that is, by the death of God incarnate, Christ our God.

5.24.1.en: He also wanted by this commandment "an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth", that a person should not repay evil with greater evil, but it is enough to repay with evil like that which befell him.

5.24.2.en: These are the commandments of the Old Testament, because the level of understanding of the people could not bear more than this.

5.24.3.en: And a person in his spiritual maturity progresses through six degrees before the evil that befalls him:

5.24.4.en: (1) Assaulting others with evil, and this is the barbaric way.

5.24.5.en: (2) Meeting evil with greater evil, because the other began with evil.

5.24.6.en: (3) Meeting evil with evil like it, and not more, as in the Jewish Law.

5.24.7.en: (4) Meeting evil with lesser evil, and this has self-control in it.

5.24.8.en: (5) Not answering evil, but keeping silent, and this is complete self-control.

5.24.9.en: (6) Meeting evil with good, and this is the Christian level, the highest of the degrees.

5.25.0.en: Christ warns us not to let the heart be agitated so as to answer evil with other evil, because if the heart is filled with love, it finds an excuse for the other, and is not disturbed by outward insult to the body, that is, the slap. The literal meaning in the slap is not what is intended, because a person is slapped on his left cheek and not the right, unless the striker is left-handed, that is, uses his left hand, so the slap falls on the right cheek. But the spiritual meaning is what is intended, which is forgiveness and endurance, indeed continuing to endure by accepting a second slap, that is, a second insult.

5.26.0.en: He gives another example in endurance and forgiveness, which is if a quarrel occurs and the other tries to seize your coat.

5.26.1.en: "Coat": it is the inner garment like a robe, and the Law ordains that no one take it because it is the covering of the poor (Ex 22:26-27).

5.26.2.en: "Cloak": it is the outer mantle, and it is more costly.

5.26.3.en: In this way we meet injustice with love, and with a gift greater than the wrongdoer wanted, however severe the injustice, so the wrongdoer is ashamed and his anger calms. And this cannot be done except from a heart full of love and satisfied with God, who easily gives up material things, even if the other thinks at first that he gained something from him and exploited him, but he stands amazed before this wonderful love, for it is a silent proclamation you offer to the wicked so that they may repent, confident that God compensates you many times over, not only in heaven but on earth as well, because His promise is clear: "There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my sake, and the gospel's, But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time ... and in the world to come eternal life" (Mk 10:29-30).

5.27.0.en: Forced labor: it is work without pay. If someone compels you to do a work, offer him a greater service, and so you win him by your love, and receive heavenly blessings.

5.27.1.en: The second mile: it is love, with which you put out the evil and injustice of others.

5.28.0.en: If you find a needy person who asks you, give to him. This is a giving up of the love of money, and a feeling for the other, and not looking at him as covetous, for his covetousness may be the result of his feeling of deprivation, so bear with him. And he may be ashamed to beg from you, so he asks for a loan while unable to repay it, so do not demand it of him, but leave it to him as a gift of love from you.

5.28.1.en: And of course, all this is according to the love that is in your heart. If you are not able to have this love, then at least bear with him and forgive him. And do not be selfish and stingy in your giving, because God said clearly: "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (v. 7).

5.28.2.en: If you believe in love, you can put out all the flame of evil in those around you, for love is stronger than hatred. Have compassion with your love on the angry and the covetous, for they are sick and need the medicine which is love, whether by bearing with them and praying for them, or speaking with them gently in place of their bad words, or offering them services; and you cannot bear with them and love them unless your heart is filled with the love of God.

5.28.3.en: So care for your spiritual relationship with God, and ask His help, and you will be able to overflow with love from Him upon others.

5.29.0.en: "Thy neighbour": in the view of the Pharisees he is the Jew, but Christ's interpretation is that he is every person, as in the parable of the Good Samaritan (Lk 10:30-37).

5.29.1.en: The Law in the Old Testament commanded love of neighbor, so that a person may come out of his selfishness and love his relatives and those close to him.

5.29.2.en: "And hate thine enemy": it is an addition by the Pharisees that the Law did not decree, and perhaps they deduced it from God's command to destroy the wicked from the Promised Land, that is, to remove evil.

5.29.3.en: Yet the Law approved helping the enemy if his donkey fell under its load (Ex 23:4-5). And it also commanded that the Edomite not be hated because he is a brother, nor the Egyptian because he was a stranger in his land, though they were among the fiercest enemies who humbled them and fought them (Deut 23:7).

5.30.0.en: With spiritual maturity in the New Testament, the Law demanded love for enemies, because their nature was created pure by God, and the evil in them is an intruder upon them from the devil. So we do not look at them as wicked, but as sick people needing love and compassion, so we bless them with kind words, and the words of evil on their lips fall silent. And by doing good with them, their hearts grow calm. And we pray for them, that God may remove from them their bad thoughts, and in this way we win them for ourselves as friends in faith and love.

5.30.1.en: "Bless": love is not limited to inner feelings, but comes out in kind and encouraging words. "Do good": love is also tied to offering services and kindnesses to those who have fallen into the case of hatred toward us. "Pray": this is the lowest degree of love, or the means that cannot be prevented, because one who is hostile to us may refuse to speak with us or accept our services, but he cannot prevent us from praying for him, however much he persecutes us.

5.31.0.en: "The children of your Father": God is love, and the proof of our sonship is that we love everyone, including the wicked and those who wrong us. By this love we become like God, who loved us and died for us on the Cross, we who disobeyed Him and defied Him and crucified Him.

5.31.1.en: And God continues in His giving to all mankind, whether those who believe in Him or those who reject Him, for He makes His sun to rise on all, and His rains water all.

5.31.2.en: And He used the sun and the rain because of their benefit to all mankind, and because they are in heaven they signify God's heavenly gifts.

5.31.3.en: If God gives light to all and satisfies all, then offer your love to everyone you meet, and forget yourself, enduring sufferings for Christ's sake, however much others wrong you.

5.32.0.en: "The publicans": they are the collectors of the Roman taxes, and are marked by greed and harshness, so they were the worst group in society, and their name is tied to sinners.

5.32.1.en: Christ declares clearly that our love for those who love us is something ordinary, which the wicked share with us, who are represented by the publicans marked by harshness and greed. But our distinction as Christians is that we love and give peace, and do good to those who wrong us and are hostile to us.

5.32.2.en: "Salute": the Law decreed not saluting the Gentiles, and limited it to the Jews, and by this the deficiency of love appears, and its not being wide enough to include all mankind, so the law of the New Testament commanded love for all.

5.33.0.en: "Be ye therefore perfect": that is, strive toward perfection.

5.33.1.en: Christ confirms that this is the perfection of love, that is, love for enemies, so that we become children of the perfect God, and He calls us to strive toward the perfection which cannot be fully reached, but God rejoices in this striving because He is the Perfect One, so this is striving toward Him.

5.33.2.en: The Sermon on the Mount continued; Spiritual practices; Detachment
